title: Convolution in two dimensions
objectives: Write a two-dimensional convolution and apply edge kernels to a small image.

screens.prose: This is a **2D convolution**: the kernel slides over rows and columns, a dot product at each stop. screens.title: Channels in
screens.prose: A colour image has 3 channels, so its input has shape $(3, 8, 8)$. Each filter then has one 3 by 3 kernel per input channel; it slides all three together and adds the three dot products into one output.
screens.question: Two such filters slide over the $(3, 8, 8)$ input. What shape is the output?

options.why: You kept a map per input channel. Each filter adds its three channels into one map.
You made one map per input channel. The number of maps is the number of filters.
Valid positions shrink each side from 8 to 6.

hints.text: How many maps does one filter make?
One: it adds its three channels together.
Two filters, each 6 by 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite. How many maps does one filter make?

explain.text: Each filter has shape $(3, 3, 3)$ and gives one map, the sum over the three channels. Two filters give two maps: $(2, 6, 6)$.

screens.title: Not a matrix product
screens.prose: A colleague computes one output of the vertical-edge kernel on a 3 by 3 patch as `patch @ K`. The patch is shown beside $\mathbf{K}$.
screens.question: What is the true output for this patch?

hints.text: Each pixel meets the weight in the same place.
Left column times $-1$, right column times $+1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pair each pixel with the weight on top of it.

byKey.matmul: You took the top-left entry of `patch @ K`, a row times a column. The window needs matching entries multiplied and all nine added.
byKey.matmul-sum: You added up `patch @ K`. A matrix product mixes rows with columns; the output pairs each pixel with its own weight.
byKey.sign: You took left minus right. The weight $+1$ is on the right-hand column.

explain.text: Elementwise: row 1 gives $0 - 1 = -1$, row 2 gives $3 - 0 = 3$, row 3 gives $1 - 2 = -1$, so the output is 1. In NumPy that is `(patch * K).sum()`, not `patch @ K`.

screens.title: A kernel of size 1 by 1
screens.prose: A 1 by 1 kernel sees one pixel at a time. On a 3-channel input it holds one weight per channel, here $(0.5, 0.25, 0.25)$, and mixes the channels at each pixel and nothing else.
screens.question: A pixel has channel values $(8, 4, 0)$. What is its output?

hints.text: Multiply each channel value by its weight.
Add the three.

feedback.generic: Not quite. One weight per channel, multiplied and added.

byKey.mean: You averaged the channels. The weights are not equal.
byKey.sum: You added the channels without their weights.

explain.text: $4 + 1 + 0 = 5$. A 1 by 1 kernel never looks at a neighbour, so it cannot find an edge; it only recombines channels, pixel by pixel.

screens.title: The two-dimensional rule
screens.prose: For an image $\mathbf{X}$ and a $k \times k$ kernel $\mathbf{K}$, unflipped: $$Y_{ij} = \sum_{a=0}^{k-1} \sum_{b=0}^{k-1} K_{ab}\, X_{i+a,\, j+b}.$$ With $c$ input channels, add over them too. The output is $(n - k + 1)$ on each side, one map per filter.
screens.question: Sixteen 3 by 3 filters slide over a $(3, 32, 32)$ input. What shape is the output?

options.why: Valid positions lose $k - 1 = 2$ on each side.
Each filter adds its 3 channels into one map, so there are 16 maps, not $16 \times 3$.
The number of maps is the number of filters, 16.

feedback.generic: Not quite. One map per filter, each side $n - k + 1$.

explain.text: Each filter has shape $(3, 3, 3)$ and makes one 30 by 30 map; sixteen filters stack into $(16, 30, 30)$.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def conv2d_valid(img, k):
    img = np.asarray(img, dtype=float)
    k = np.asarray(k, dtype=float)
    kh, kw = k.shape
    oh, ow = img.shape[0] - kh + 1, img.shape[1] - kw + 1
    out = np.zeros((oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            out[i, j] = np.sum(img[i:i + kh, j:j + kw] * k)
    return out

ideas: In 2D the kernel slides over rows and columns; an $n \times n$ image and a $k \times k$ kernel give $(n - k + 1) \times (n - k + 1)$ valid outputs.
